Chapter 6, Ātmasaṃyamayoga, "the yoga of self-restraint," is the Gītā's fullest manual of meditation. It opens by redefining renunciation and yoga as one and the same thing — not abstention from the sacrificial fire or from action, but performing one's duty without attachment to its fruit — and pictures the self as either one's best friend or one's worst enemy, depending on whether it has been mastered. From there Kṛṣṇa gives concrete instructions: a solitary, moderate life; a firm seat of cloth, hide, and kuśa-grass, neither too high nor too low; an erect, motionless posture with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose; and a mind drawn back, again and again, patiently, whenever it wanders, until it rests in the self alone, as steady as a lamp in a windless place. The state this practice reaches is described first as an equal vision that sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, then, more personally, as a bond in which Kṛṣṇa is never lost to the one who sees him everywhere. Arjuna objects that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and then asks what becomes of a practitioner who has faith but fails to complete the discipline before death. Kṛṣṇa answers that no effort on this path is ever wasted: such a person is reborn into circumstances that let him resume his practice from where he left off, and, striving across many lifetimes if need be, eventually reaches the highest goal. The chapter closes by ranking the yogin above the ascetic, the man of mere learning, and the ritual performer alike, and above all other yogins by naming the one whose inmost self is fixed on Kṛṣṇa in faith and devotion as the most disciplined of all.
